topics.title: The need to count: natural numbers

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how one-to-one correspondence allowed early humans to count and record quantities.
Identify early evidence of number use such as the Ishango bone and the Vedic names for powers of 10.
Decide whether natural numbers are closed under a given operation, using counterexamples.
Describe how the idea of shunyata and the Bakhshali manuscript led to zero as a number.
Apply Brahmagupta's rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying with zero.
Describe integers as fortunes (dhana), debts (rina) and zero, and the symbol Z.
Use Brahmagupta's rules of signs to add, subtract and multiply integers in real-life contexts.
State the definition of a rational number p/q and explain why q must not be zero.
Test whether two rational numbers are equal using the rule ad = bc.
Add, subtract, multiply and divide rational numbers and use their closure properties.

topics.title: Rationals on the number line, absolute value and density

concepts.learning_objective: Locate rational numbers on the number line by dividing unit intervals into equal parts.
Find absolute values and the distance |a - b| between two rational numbers.
Find rational numbers between two given rationals using averages and explain density.
Follow the proof by contradiction that the square root of 2 is irrational.
Construct lengths such as the square roots of 2 and 3 on the number line using right triangles.
Describe pi as irrational and evaluate partial sums of Madhava's series.
Predict from the denominator's prime factors whether a rational number's decimal terminates or repeats.
Convert pure and general repeating decimals into the form p/q.
Distinguish rational and irrational numbers by their decimal expansions and describe the real numbers.
